newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Unemployment sours bright world economic outlook.
newsitem.headline: Unemployment sours bright world economic outlook.

text.p: Members of the international and political elite head home from the World Economic Forum on Tuesday optimistic about the global economy but anxious about prospects for European jobs.

With Asian economies outside Japan judged buoyant, the U.S. still steaming ahead and Europe showing clear signs of escaping the doldrums of the mid-1990s, the picture painted at the week-long gathering was as bright as the Swiss mountain scenery.
Inflation seemed under control and, just as importantly, there appeared to be near unanimity among the world's decision-makers that letting prices rip offered no quick fix for a sluggish economy.

The threat to trade from protectionism, once a key concern at the annual get-togethers between political leaders, captains of industry and top academics in this ski resort, was also fading as a fear, they said.

"For the first time in 10 years of attending these informal talks...there was no widespread fear of protectionism and there was a conviction that any financial crisis could be managed," said former U.S. senator Bill Bradley, official rapporteur to the 1997 conference.

Overall, the world economy should expand by around four percent in 1997. Output in the European Union would quicken to some 2.5 percent from less than two percent last year, pulled along by declining interest rates, according to Horst Siebert, president of Germany's Kiel Institute for World Economics.
But the bad news was that faster growth would do nothing to cut the job queues in Europe, particularly in France and Germany with unemployment in the latter at an all-time high of over four million.
"The world can be optimistic, but Europe is faced with the unemployment problem and this puts some sourness into an otherwise optimistic picture," said Siebert.
"Growth and unemployment are completely uncoupled. We can no longer hope that economic growth can reduce unemployment," he said.
The only solution to getting Europeans back to work lay in reforming the continent's often restrictive labour laws to introduce greater flexibility in wages and work times and more worker mobility.

But the doubt was whether politicians and their electorate were yet prepared to bite the bullet and accept reforms that would reduce the security of those in jobs to give a greater chance to those seeking work, participants said.
"The political process -- governments and opposition -- have not yet agreed on this and the population has not yet accepted some of the necessary changes," said Siebert.

The need was becoming even more pressing with the introduction of the single currency in the European Union from 1999 because jobs and wages would take the role of exchange rates in regulating crises in individual member states.

But U.S. union leader John Sweeney, president of the AFL-CIO federation, warned against European countries rushing to imitate the U.S., where easy hire-and-fire laws and high labour mobility are often cited as the secret of its low unemployment rates.
There was a downside to the U.S. experience which was all too often forgotten, he said.

In the past 16 years, 43 million jobs had been eliminated in the United States through mass lay-offs by major corporations. While most had found other jobs, two-thirds of them were for less money, Sweeney said.
"Families and communities are disrupted as profitable plants close...the majority of working people are working harder and longer just to stay even," he warned.
